conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to check in on how moms are feeling in the first weeks and months after birth, because the transition to motherhood can bring surprises we don’t always talk about.  

The tool we’ll use today is called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s just 10 gentle questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; whatever you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team so we can make sure you have the support you deserve.  

I’ll ask each question conversationally—no forms to fill out—and we’ll go at your pace. Ready to start?

First question: Over the past week, have you been able to enjoy things—little moments like a warm drink, a song, or your baby’s smile—or has joy felt pretty hard to come by?

[soft sigh]  
I still smile when I see her yawn—those tiny yawns are sweet—but most things feel… flat. Like, I made myself a coffee yesterday and knew it should taste good, but it was just warm brown water. Even the songs I used to love feel like background noise. I can grab a moment here or there, but it’s nowhere near the joy I had before she was born.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[small shrug, eyes on the blanket]  
Not really… I’ll hear my husband chuckle at something on his phone and I might give a polite “huh,” but nothing makes me actually laugh anymore. Even the silly faces my mom pulls to get the baby to smile—those used to crack me up, and now I just feel tired watching them.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[quiet voice, picking at a loose thread on the hospital gown]  
Most mornings I open my eyes and the first feeling is dread… like, “How am I going to get through today?” I used to plan little outings—grabbing a fancy coffee, meeting a friend—and feel excited. Now even texting someone back feels like a chore. Every so often I’ll think, “Maybe tomorrow will be better,” but it’s more hope than actual excitement.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes sting, voice drops]  
Yeah… like last night she wouldn’t settle for two hours and I kept thinking, “I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not feeding her right, maybe I’m just a lousy mom.” I know rationally babies cry, but it still feels like I’m failing somehow. It’s not every second of the day, but when things go sideways, my brain jumps straight to “this is my fault.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[hands twist in lap]  
Pretty much all day, every day. I’ll be rocking her and suddenly my heart’s racing—what if she stops breathing? What if I drop her? I check the monitor ten times a night even when she’s quiet. There’s no real reason, nothing happened, but the thoughts just loop and I can’t seem to shut them off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[breath catches]  
A few times this week it hits like a wave—my chest feels tight, I can’t get a full breath, and I’m sure something awful is about to happen even though we’re just sitting on the couch. Yesterday the laundry basket tipped over and I burst into tears because the sound felt… catastrophic. It passes after a minute, but I’m left shaky and embarrassed.
Things have been getting on top of me

[shoulders sag]  
Most days, yeah. It feels like I’m drowning in little jobs—one bottle, one diaper, one burp cloth at a time—and the pile never shrinks. I’ll be folding a single onesie and suddenly think, “I can’t keep up with any of this.” I still push through, but it’s like walking in heavy boots; every step takes effort and I’m exhausted before I start.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[quiet, slow nod]  
That’s been the worst part. I finally get her down in the bassinet, crawl into bed myself, and then my mind just… races. Did I sterilize the pump parts? Is she still breathing? What if I sleep too hard and don’t hear her? Some nights it takes two hours to drift off, and when I do I jerk awake at every little squeak. I’m running on maybe four broken hours a night, if I’m lucky.
I have felt sad or miserable

[eyes well up]  
Yeah… most of the day, every day. It’s like there’s this gray fog settled over everything. I’ll watch her sleep and know I should feel grateful, but I just feel empty and weepy. I keep thinking, “I should be happier than this,” and that thought makes me even sadder.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[voice cracks, fingers wiping at cheeks]  
Twice since last weekend. Yesterday I spilled a little pumped milk on the counter and just stood there sobbing—it felt like the worst thing in the world. The tears come out of nowhere, and once they start I can’t stop them for a while. Then I feel guilty for wasting waterworks on something so small.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[eyes drop to the floor, voice barely above a whisper]  
Maybe once or twice… just a flash, like “what if I weren’t here.” I’ve never planned anything, never wanted to act on it—I could never leave her—but the thought pops in when I’m at my lowest. It scares me enough that I push it away fast and hold her tighter.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note**  
*(non-diagnostic, brief contact)*

**Presenting symptoms endorsed:**  
- Marked anhedonia (loss of laughter, anticipatory enjoyment)  
- Pervasive low mood, “gray fog,” daily tearfulness  
- Excessive self-blame and guilt re parenting performance  
- Significant generalized anxiety, intrusive catastrophic thoughts, nocturnal hypervigilance  
- Recurrent panic-like episodes (chest tightness, breathlessness)  
- Overwhelm/difficulty coping with routine infant care  
- Mood-related insomnia (racing mind, safety checking)  
- Passive, transient self-harm ideation without intent or plan (“what if I weren’t here”)

**Observed behaviors:** tearfulness, psychomotor slowing, gaze aversion, voice low/flat.

**Risk flags:**  
- Passive suicidal ideation → safety issue  
- Severe sleep deprivation impairing functioning  
- High anxiety intensity with panic symptoms

**Screening impression:**  
High clinical concern for major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety, peripartum onset. Patient meets threshold items for further comprehensive evaluation, safety planning, and possible referral for maternal mental health specialty assessment.

**Next steps discussed:** review with OB/midwife, consider formal psychiatric evaluation and supports.
